title: A Case Study: Freedom from Suffering
author: Zhiyu
excerpt: There is no future; no light at the end of the tunnel; both ends seem blocked, and you are trapped inside.

inline.s: There is no future; there is no light at the end of the tunnel; both ends seem blocked, and you are trapped inside.

If I had known earlier that the future would be far brighter than everything I had experienced before, that end of the tunnel would have been blown to pieces, and I would have been able to see the light.

To escape that monster, you keep running and running. But this is useless: you cannot keep your back turned to it forever. You must turn around bravely, and only then can you see the monster's true face.
The mind is always making up stories. Do not identify with it, and do not follow it. That is a daydream — wake up at once!
A long illness makes a skilled physician; be your own therapist — this is the surest of all strategies.
It takes the one who tied the bell to untie it.

[It takes the one who tied the bell to untie it] One day Chan Master Fayan asked the assembly: “Who can untie the golden bell around the tiger's neck?” None could answer. Taiqin happened to arrive, and Fayan put the question to him. Taiqin said: “The one who tied it can untie it.”
In
A New Earth: Awakening to Your Life's Purpose
, Eckhart
Tolle writes:

A woman in her thirties came to see me. As she greeted me, I could sense the pain behind her polite and superficial smile. She began to tell her story, and within a second her smile turned into a grimace of pain. Then she began to sob uncontrollably. She said she felt lonely and empty, with much anger and sadness. When she was little, she had been physically abused by her father.
I quickly saw that
her pain was not caused by the conditions of her present life
, but by an unusually powerful pain-body. Her pain-body had become a
filter
through which she viewed her life situation. She could not see the
connection
between her emotional pain and her thoughts, because she was completely identified with both. She could also not see that she was
feeding

her pain-body with her thoughts. In other words, she lived with a burden — namely, a deeply unhappy self. Yet on some level she must have realized that her pain originated from herself, and that she was a burden to herself. She was ready to awaken, and that is why she had come to me.
I guided her to focus on the sensations within her body
, and at the same time asked her to
directly
feel the emotion, rather than feeling it through the
filter

of her unhappy thoughts and unhappy story. She said she had come expecting me to teach her how to escape from her unhappiness, not to enter into it. Yet she reluctantly did what I asked. Tears rolled down her face, and her whole body trembled. “This is what you feel at this moment,” I said. “About this fact before you, you can do nothing, because this is what you are feeling right now. Now, if you wish this moment were different, you are only adding more pain to the pain you already have. So, can you
completely accept
that this is what you feel right now?”
She fell silent for a while. Suddenly she became very impatient, as if about to stand up, and said angrily: “No! I will not accept this!”
“Who is speaking?” I asked her. “Is it you, or the unhappiness within you? Can you see that your unhappiness about being unhappy is yet another layer of unhappiness?”
She fell silent again.

“I am not asking you to do anything. I am only asking you to see whether you can allow these emotions to be there. In other words, strange as it may sound, if you did not mind your unhappiness, what would happen to your unhappiness? Don't you want to find out?”

She was briefly puzzled, and sat quietly for a minute or so. I suddenly noticed a marked shift in her energy field. She said: “It's strange. I am still unhappy, but now there is space around it, and it doesn't seem so important anymore.”

This was the first time I had heard anyone describe it that way: there is space around my unhappiness. Of course, that space appeared because inwardly she was able to accept everything she was experiencing in the present moment.
I said nothing more, allowing her to remain with the experience. After a while, she came to see that when she
stopped identifying with
the feeling — that old painful emotion living inside her — and placed her attention directly on the emotion without trying to resist it,
it could no longer control her thoughts
and become mixed up with the story of the so-called “unhappy me” fabricated by the mind. Another dimension beyond her personal past (namely,
the dimension of presence
) entered her life. Without an unhappy story, you cannot be unhappy, so this was the end of her unhappiness.
It was also the beginning of the end of her pain-body
. The emotion itself is not unhappiness;
only the emotion plus an unhappy story
constitutes unhappiness.
When our conversation ended, I was satisfied to have witnessed in another person the
rising of presence

. The primary reason we exist in human form is to bring that dimension of consciousness into the world. I had also witnessed the diminishment of the pain-body, not through fighting it, but by bringing in the light of consciousness.

Not all unhappiness comes from the pain-body. Some new unhappiness arises when you are not in harmony with the present moment, refusing or denying the Now in some form. When you realize that the present moment already is, and is inescapable, then inwardly you will willingly say to it:
“Yes!”
and accept it. Then no more unhappiness will be created. And when your
inner resistance
has dissolved, you will be empowered by life itself.
(For details, please watch
“The Astonishing Power of Yes (Video)”

Non-resistance does not necessarily mean doing nothing; it means that whatever one does does not arise from habitual reaction. Think about it: which is more effective — action taken in a state of resentment, or action taken calmly and objectively?
Moreover, the resistance produced toward an event is the root of suffering;
the negative emotions and excessive actions it produces usually do far greater harm to body and mind, career, and relationships than the event itself.
When you are in a state of intense presence and “do nothing,” this is a powerful force of transformation and healing for situations and people.
In
Practicing the Power of Now
, Eckhart
Tolle writes:
(If you want to be free of unhappiness,)
begin by acknowledging the resistance within you

When resistance arises, stay with it and observe how your mind creates it, and how it labels situations, yourself, or other people. Look at the thinking process involved, and feel the energy of the emotion.
By witnessing the resistance, you will find that it is utterly useless;
by focusing your full attention on the Now
, the unconscious resistance becomes conscious, and that is its end.
You cannot be both conscious and unhappy, both conscious and in a negative state. Negativity, unhappiness, or suffering, in whatever form it appears, means there is
resistance
present, and resistance is always
unconscious
Even if you are aware of your unhappy feelings, the fact is that you have
identified
with them and, through
compulsive thinking

, kept the process going — all of it unconsciously. If you are conscious, that is, if you are fully present in the Now, then all negativity will disappear almost at once. It cannot survive in your presence; it can only live on in your absence.
At the level of Being
(self-nature)
, all suffering is seen as illusion.
Suffering arises because of identification with form.
Miracles of healing sometimes happen through this realization: awakening in others the
consciousness of Being
— if they are ready.
[Identification] Taking forms to be real, and dividing them into “mine” and “not mine.”
The brain
(the mind)
is your tool for surviving in the world of form;
it should be you who controls it, not it that controls you.
On the wisdom of surrender, Eckhart
Tolle writes in
Practicing the Power of Now
What kind of future you experience depends largely on the quality of consciousness in this present moment. Therefore,
surrender
is the most important thing for bringing about positive change. Any action you take is secondary; true positive action cannot arise from a state of consciousness that is not surrendered.

For some people, surrender may have a negative connotation, suggesting defeat, giving up, inability to withstand life's challenges, becoming passive, sluggish, and so on. However, true surrender is completely different from all that. It does not mean passively enduring every situation you are in, doing nothing, nor does it mean stopping your plans or failing to take positive action.

Surrender is a simple but profound wisdom — going with the flow of life rather than against it. The only moment in which you can experience the flow of life is the Now, so surrender is unconditional, unreserved acceptance of the present moment.
It is letting go of the inner resistance to what is.

Inner resistance is saying “no” to what is through mental judgment and negative emotion — this is especially evident when things go wrong. What is called “going wrong” is the gap between your mind's demands or rigid expectations and what is.
It is this gap that produces suffering.

If you live long enough, you will know that things go wrong all day long. If you want to remove pain and sorrow from your life, then it is precisely when things go wrong that you most need to practice surrender. Accepting what is will immediately release you from identification with the mind, and thereby reconnect you with Being.
Resistance is the mind.
Surrender is a purely inner phenomenon; it does not mean that you cannot take action on the outer level and change the situation.

In fact, when you surrender, what you need to accept is not the whole situation, but the tiny segment called the Now. For example, if you are stuck deep in the mud, you might say: “All right, I resign myself to it, I'll just stay stuck in the mud.” But resignation is not surrender.

You do not need to accept an unpleasant life situation, nor deceive yourself by saying there is nothing wrong with it. You can wholeheartedly acknowledge that you want to leave the situation, and then focus your attention on the present moment, without labeling it mentally in any way.
This means there is no judgment of the Now, hence no resistance and no negative emotion; you accept the “suchness” of this present moment.
Then you can take action, doing your best to get yourself out of that situation.

I call such action positive action; it is far more effective than negative action born of anger, despair, or frustration. Until you achieve the result you want, keep practicing surrender by not labeling the Now.
The wondrous remedy for suffering: presence.
Unless you truly
practice surrender
, this spiritual dimension will remain merely something you read about, talk about, get excited about, write books about, think about, believe in, or disbelieve. It will not make any difference.
Only when you can truly surrender will this spiritual dimension become a living reality in your life.
The intensity of suffering depends on the degree of your resistance to the Now,
and the degree of your resistance to the Now depends on the degree of your identification with the mind.

[The mind] The thinking of the brain — the thinker. In Eckhart Tolle's Practicing the Power of Now and other works, the original word is “mind.” [Identification with the mind] Believing that the mind (the thinker) is who you truly are. Practicing the Power of Now opens by saying: “The first step toward freedom is to realize that you are not the thinker.”
The process by which suffering arises and persists:
falling into unconsciousness → identifying with the mind → resisting the Now → compulsive thinking.
Therefore, the key to freedom from suffering is:
being conscious → not identifying with the mind → surrendering to the Now → cutting off compulsive thinking.

[Compulsive thinking] A vicious cycle of thinking that cannot be stopped. Compulsive thinking not only makes you suffer greatly, but also gives rise to many mental and physical illnesses. As the saying goes: the moment the skandha of perception arises, the demon finds its opportunity.
So, whenever you find yourself suffering, immediately alert yourself: “I am daydreaming again!” Then, with undivided attention, be present and observe the thinker,
surrender to the Now, cut off compulsive thinking, and wake from the dream.

Question: I also know I should cut off compulsive thinking. But the problem is that, although I keep telling myself, “Stop thinking! Stop thinking!” I still can't stop thinking, and the torment goes on. What should I do?

Answer: it is called “compulsive thinking” precisely because it is delusion that arises on its own and cannot be stopped. To cut it off at once requires a certain power of concentration. For this, you can practice according to
Practicing the Power of Now
, to develop the concentration of presence (abiding in the Now), and cut off compulsive thinking by observing the thinker. If you still cannot cut it off, I suggest you also practice according to
Chan of Awareness
or
Investigating Buddha-Recitation
, and you will surely cut it off.
Place more attention on the “doing” itself,
rather than on the result you want to achieve through doing it.
Whatever the present moment brings forth,
be wholly absorbed in it.
